div.head: SUBSECT. 3.
Of Witches and Magicians, how they cause Melancholy.
div.p: You have heard what the Devil can do of himself, now you shall hear what he can perform by his instruments, who are many times worse (if it be possible) than he himself, and to satisfy their revenge and lust, cause more mischief, Multa enim mala non egisse daemon, nisi provocatus a Sagis, as De Lamiis.Erastus thinks, much harm had never been done, had he not been provoked by Witches to it. He had not appeared in Samuel’s shape, if the Witch of Endor had let him alone; or represented those Serpents in Pharaoh’s presence, had not the Magicians urged him unto it: Nec morbos vel hominibus, vel brutis infligeret (Erastus maintains), si Sagae quiescerent; men and cattle might go free; if the Witches would let him alone. Many deny Witches at all, or if there be any, they can do no harm; of this opinion is Wierus, lib. 3 cap. 53 de praestig. daem., Austin Lercheimer a Dutch Writer, Biermannus, Ewichius, Neuwaldus, our Countryman Scot; with him in Horace,

they laugh at all such Stories; but on the contrary are most Lawyers, Divines, Physicians, Philosophers, Austin, Hemmingius, Danaeus, Chytraeus, Zanchius, Aretius, &c., Delrio, Sprenger, Et quomodo venefici fiant enarrat [And he explains how sorcerers are created].Niderius lib. 5 Formicar., Cujatius, Bartolus, consil. 6 tom. 1, Bodin daemonoman. lib. 2 cap. 8, Godelman, Damhoderius, &c., Paracelsus, Erastus, Scribonius, Camerarius, &c. The parties by whom the Devil deals, may be reduced to these two, such as command him in show at least, as Conjurers, and Magicians, whose detestable and horrid mysteries are contained in their book called De quo plura legas in [Of which you can read much more in] Boissardo lib. 1 de praestig.Arbatel; daemones enim advocati praesto sunt, seque exorcismis & conjurationibus quasi cogi patiuntur, ut miserum
magorum genus in impietate detineant [for the demons show themselves when they are called, and permit themselves to be, as it were, compelled by exorcisms and spells, in order to detain the miserable order of magicians in impiety]. Or such as are commanded, as Witches, that deal ex parte implicite, or explicite, as the Rex Jacobus Daemonol. lib. 1 cap. 3.King hath well defined; many subdivisions there are, and many several species of Sorcerers, Witches, Enchanters, Charmers, &c. They have been tolerated heretofore some of them; and Magic hath been publicly professed in former times, in An University in Spain in old Castile.Salamanca, The chief town in Poland.Cracovia, and other places, though after censured by several Oxford and Paris, see finem [at the end] P. Lumbardi.Universities, and now generally contradicted, though practised by some still, maintained and excused, tanquam res secreta quae non nisi viris magnis & peculiari beneficio de Coelo instructis communicatur [as if it were a secret matter communicated only to great men and those provided with a special privilege from heaven] (I use Praefat. de magis & veneficis lib.Boissardus his words), and so far approved by some Princes, ut nihil ausi aggredi in politicis, in sacris, in consiliis, sine eorum arbitrio [that they’ve dared to undertake nothing in politics, in sacred matters, in councils, without their opinion]; they consult still with them, and dare indeed do nothing without their advice. Nero and Heliogabalus, Maxentius, and Julianus Apostata, were never so much addicted to Magic of old, as some of our modern Princes and Popes themselves are nowadays. Ericus King of Sweden, had an enchanted Cap, by virtue of which and some magical murmur or whispering terms he could command spirits, trouble the air, and make the wind stand which way he would, insomuch that when there was any great wind or storm, the common people were wont to say, the King now had on his conjuring Cap. But such examples are infinite. That which they can do, is as much almost as the devil himself, who is still ready to satisfy their desires, to oblige them the more unto him. They can cause tempests, storms, which is familiarly practised by Witches in Norway, Iceland, as I have proved. They can make friends enemies, and enemies friends by philtres; Erastus.turpes amores conciliare [provoke shameful desires], enforce love, tell any man where his friends are, about what employed, though in the most remote places; and if they will, bring their sweethearts to them by night, upon a Goat’s back flying in the air. Sigismund Scherertzius, part. 1 cap. 9 de spect., reports confidently, that he conferred with sundry such, that had been so carried many miles, and that he heard Witches themselves confess as much; hurt, and infect men and beasts, Vines, Corn, Cattle, Plants, make Women abortive, not to conceive, Vide Petrum de Palude lib. 4 distinct. 34. Paulum Grillandum.barren, men and women unapt and unable, married and unmarried, fifty several ways, saith Bodin lib. 2 cap. 2, fly in the air, meet when and where they will, as Cicogna proves, & Lavat. de spect. part. 2 cap. 17, steal young children out of their cradles, ministerio daemonum [with the help of demons], and put deformed in their rooms, which we call Changelings, saith Scherertzius, part. 1 cap. 6, make men
victorious, fortunate, eloquent; & therefore in those ancient Milles.Monomachies and combats they were searched of old, they had no Magical charms; they can make Dr. Luther, in primum praeceptum, & Leon. Vairus lib. 1 de Fascino.stick-frees, such as shall endure a Rapier’s point, Musket shot, and never be wounded: of which read more in Boissardus cap. 6 de Magia, the manner of the adjuration, and by whom ’tis made, where and how to be used in expeditionibus bellicis, praeliis, duellis, &c. [on military expeditions, in battles, duels, etc.], with many peculiar instances and examples; they can walk in fiery furnaces, make men feel no pain on the Rack, aut alias torturas sentire [or when enduring other tortures]; they can staunch blood, Lavater. Cicog.represent dead men’s shapes, Erastus.alter and turn themselves and others into several forms, at their pleasures. Boissardus de Magis.Agaberta a famous Witch in Lapland, would do as much publicly to all spectators, modo Pusilla, modo anus, modo procera ut quercus, modo vacca, avis, coluber, &c., now young, now old, high, low, like a Cow, like a Bird, a Snake, and what not? She could represent to others what forms they most desired to see, show them friends absent, reveal secrets, maxima omnium admiratione, &c. [to the greatest astonishment of everyone, etc.] And yet for all this subtlety of theirs, as Lipsius well observes, Physiolog. Stoicor. lib. 1 cap. 17, neither these Magicians nor devils themselves, can take away Gold or Letters out of mine or Crassus’ Chest, & clientelis suis largiri [and lavish them upon their followers], for they are base, poor, contemptible fellows most part; as Daemon. lib. 3 cap. 3.Bodin notes, they can do nothing in Judicum decreta aut poenas, in regum Concilia vel arcana, nihil in rem nummariam aut thesauros, they cannot give money to their Clients, alter Judges’ decrees, or Councils of Kings, these minuti Genii [petty spirits] cannot do it, altiores Genii hoc sibi adservarunt, the higher powers reserve these things to themselves. Now and then peradventure there may be some more famous Magicians like Simon Magus, Vide Philostratum vita ejus.Apollonius Tyaneus, Vide Suidam de Paset.Pasetes, Vide Boissardum de Magis.Iamblichus, Nubrigensem lege lib. 1 cap. 19.Eudo de Stellis, that for a time can build Castles in the air, represent armies, &c., as they are De Cruent. Cadaver.said to have done, command wealth and treasure, feed thousands with all variety of meats upon a sudden, protect themselves and their followers from all Princes’ persecutions, by removing from place to place in an instant, reveal secrets, future events, tell what is done in far Countries, make them appear that died long since, &c., and do many such miracles, to the world’s terror, admiration and opinion of Deity to themselves, yet the Devil forsakes them at last, they come to wicked ends, and raro aut nunqum [rarely or never] such Impostors are to be found. The vulgar sort of them can work no such feats. But to my purpose, they can, last of all, Adolphus Scribonius.cure and cause most diseases to
such as they love or hate, & this of Virg. Aeneid. 4 incantatricem describens: Haec se carminibus promittit solvere mentes: quas velit, ast aliis duras immittere curas [describing an enchantress: ‘With her incantations she promises to release those souls she chooses, but to send severe troubles to others’].Melancholy amongst the rest. Paracelsus Tom. 4 de morbis amentium, Tract. 1, in express words affirms, Multi fascinantur in melancholiam, many are bewitched into melancholy, out of his experience. The same, saith Danaeus lib. 3 de sortiariis, Vidi, inquit, qui Melancholicos morbos gravissimos induxerunt: I have seen [he says] those that have caused Melancholy in the most grievous manner, Godelmannus cap. 7 lib. 1.dried up women’s Paps, cured Gout, Palsy; this and Apoplexy, Falling sickness, which no Physic could help, solo tactu, by touch alone. Ruland in his 3rd Cent. Cura 91 gives an instance of one David Helde a young man, who by eating Cakes which a Witch gave him, mox delirare caepit, began to dote on a sudden, and was instantly mad: F. H. D. in Factus inde Maniacus [Thence he became a maniac], spic. 2 fol. 187.Hildesheim, consulted about a Melancholy man, thought his disease was partly Magical, and partly natural, because he vomited pieces of iron and lead, and spake such Languages, as he had never been taught; but such examples are common in Scribonius, Hercules de Saxonia, and others. The means by which they work, are usually Charms, images, as that in Hector Boethius of King Duff; characters stamped of sundry metals, and at such and such constellations, knots, amulets, words, Philtres, &c., which generally make the parties affected, melancholy; as Omnia Philtra etsi inter differant hoc habent commune, quo hominem efficiant melancholicum [All philtres, though they may differ among themselves, have this in common: that they make a man melancholic], epist. 231 Scholtzii.Monavius discourseth at large in an Epistle of his to Acholzius, giving instance in a Bohemian Baron that was so troubled by a Philtre taken. Not that there is any power at all in those spells, charms, characters, and barbarous words; but that the Devil doth use such means to delude them. Ut fideles inde magos (saith De cruent. Cadaver.Libavius) in officio retineat, tum in consortium malefactorum vocet [So that he can thereby hold the faithful magicians … to their duty, then summon them to the fellowship of evil-doers].
